en: The Small Chamber, Six Gates, Part 1:
Verse on the Heart Sūtra, Gate One. Verse on the Heart of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
The ocean of wisdom is pure;
its principles are subtle and its meanings profound.
Having reached the other shore, one attains *pāramitā*.
Turning toward the Way depends solely upon the mind;
though one may have heard a thousand kinds of teachings,
they are no more than a needle separated from its thread.
A single thread of the Flower Sutra,
revered by the multitude of sages for ten thousand kalpas—
this is Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva transcends noble wisdom;
the six sense bases are entirely identical.
With a mind empty, he contemplates with sovereign mastery.
With unimpeded great supernormal powers,
they enter meditative absorption through the gates of dhyāna;
in samādhi, they move freely in all directions.
Having traveled throughout the ten directions,
one does not see the traces of the Buddha's path.
When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, [one perceives this].
For six years he sought the Great Way;
practicing the profound, it never left his person.
Through wisdom, his mind attained liberation.
The leader who has reached the further shore;
the Noble Path is empty and profoundly still—
thus have I now heard.
The Buddha acts with impartiality;
when the time arrives, he naturally transcends the multitudes.
He perceives that the five aggregates are all empty.
Through craving, the five aggregates are formed;
their provisional union constitutes the body.
Flesh and blood are joined by sinews and bones.
A heap of dust within the skin;
deluded followers give rise to attachment,
while the wise do not treat it as kin.
The four marks all return to extinction;
that which is called "Extinction" is the True.
It delivers one from all suffering and calamity.
Falsely binding the body as suffering,
one’s own mind is deluded by the notion of self and others;
this is the pure path to nirvāṇa.
Who would be willing to set their heart upon it?
Arising from the aggregates, elements, and six sense objects,
they are followed by the signs of calamity and karma.
If you wish for the mind to be free from suffering,
hear this and awaken early to Bodhi. Śāriputra!
The realization of the Way originates from the mind;
when the mind is pure, its benefits are manifold.
It is like a lotus flower emerging from the water.
Suddenly awakening to the source of the Way and its harmony,
one constantly abides in the state of quiescent extinction;
such wisdom is difficult for the multitudes to surpass.
Transcending alone beyond the three realms,
one no longer yearns for this Sahā world;
form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form.
Form and emptiness are of one kind;
it is only upon failing to see them as such that they appear as two.
It is the followers of the Two Vehicles who give rise to such discrimination.
Grasping at signs deceives one's own mind;
outside of emptiness, there is no separate form.
The meaning of "non-form" is thus expansive.
The nature of non-arising is purity;
for one who realizes this, it is nirvana.
Form is itself emptiness.
Emptiness is itself form;
it is not that emptiness is absent because of emptiness.
It is not that form is formless because of form.
Form and emptiness return to the same unity;
the Pure Land attains peace and tranquility.
It is not that emptiness is empty; it is this very state that is wondrous.
Neither form nor non-form are distinct;
both form and emptiness are without marks.
Where, then, can a physical body be established?
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Feeling and perception receive various conditions;
mental formations and consciousness have the capacity for broad discernment.
The mind of pervasive conceptualization must be extinguished;
my illness does not concern you.
The mind of liberation is unimpeded.
By shattering attachments, one awakens to the source of the mind;
thus it is said, "It is also like this.
Nature and appearance are of one and the same essence.
Śāriputra, regarding the explanation of the characteristics of the body of the *śailagāthā*,
it is said that "beneficial speech is of a single nature of mind."
The Bodhisattva’s adamantine power prevents the four marks from causing encroachment;
having realized the Way, one is free from attachment to persons.
Upon seeing the nature of reality, dharmas are without sound;
all outflows are completely exhausted,
and the entire body is true gold.
These dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness;
the Buddhas teach the dharma of emptiness,
yet the śrāvakas seek it with [notions of] characteristics.
Seeking through the sutras and investigating the principles,
on what day shall my study of the mind cease?
May I realize the perfected, true nature.
Suddenly seeing that the mind has ceased its cultivation,
one transcends the dharma-realm in utter isolation;
being thus sovereign, what further cause for anxiety could there be?
Neither arising nor ceasing,
the pure essence of Vairocana is formless and primordially true.
Like space, it is all-pervasive;
its essence endures for ten thousand kalpas.
It is unique and remains unattached to anything.
Without old and without new,
blending with the light of the mundane world yet unstained by it,
you alone are the Honored One within the three realms.
Neither defiled nor pure;
True Suchness transcends the triple world.
Defilement and purity have been non-existent from the very beginning.
The Muni employs skillful means to speak of the subtle and the coarse;
yet in the realm of emptiness, no phenomena exist.
This manifests as a solitary wheel;
originally there was not even a single thing.
How could it be appropriate to call it two kinds?
Neither increasing nor decreasing,
the Tathāgata’s essence is signless,
filling the emptiness of the ten directions.
Existence cannot be established atop emptiness;
within existence, emptiness is not seen.
It appears like the moon reflected in water.
Hearing is like the wind passing by one's ear;
how could the Dharmakāya increase or decrease?
The Three Realms are called its true form.
Therefore, within emptiness,
awakening does not exist externally;
it is difficult to find even by seeking within.
Neither with marks nor without marks;
the measuring faculty loses its function.
The world is not the world.
The three lights illuminate the four heavens;
fundamentally there is no obstruction.
Where, then, could there be any hindrance?
There is no form, nor sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Form is originally empty;
sensation and the mind are likewise the same.
The consciousness of formations has no intermediate state;
when existence is exhausted, one returns to emptiness.
Clinging to existence as real, it is not truly existent.
Relying on emptiness, one again falls into emptiness;
only when both form and mind are transcended does one finally attain supernatural powers.
There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
The six sense faculties lack intrinsic nature;
they are merely arranged according to their appearances.
The faculty of sight distinguishes forms;
the tongue of man and self engages in jesting;
the nose may distinguish fragrances and stenches.
When the desires of body and mind diverge,
craving for the six sense bases is severed;
for ten thousand kalpas, one shall not transmigrate in saṃsāra.
There is no form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental object;
in realized wisdom there is neither sound nor form.
Who else could there be for odor, taste, or touch?
The six sense objects arise from delusion;
the ordinary mind is naturally mired in confusion and doubt.
Cease birth-and-death within birth-and-death.
At the moment of realizing Bodhi,
the nature of phenomena is empty and non-abiding;
one only fears that awakening others may be delayed.
There is no眼界 (eye-element) up to and including no意識界 (consciousness-element).
The six consciousnesses arise from delusion;
the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) opens of itself.
The eyes, ears, body, and mind—
who would dare to exercise self-restraint?
The tongue and nose act in a state of perversion.
The mind-king sends them back;
they do not remain long among the six consciousnesses.
They suddenly awaken toward the Tathāgata.
There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance; and so on, up to: there is no old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death.
When the twelve links of dependent origination exist, birth arises, followed by the characteristics of old age.
When the ignorance regarding the body arises,
the two aspects reach equality at their head;
when the body is exhausted, ignorance is exhausted.
The time for receiving retribution has arrived;
the wisdom-body is like an illusion.
Hasten to awaken to the unconditioned.
There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path;
the Four Truths arise within the triple world.
The meaning of the Sudden Teaching is clear and distinct.
Suffering is severed and its origin extinguished;
the Noble Path is spontaneously accomplished.
The Śrāvaka rests from conceptual proliferation.
The mind of the Pratyekabuddha is at peace;
if you wish to know the place of Buddhahood,
let nothing remain lingering upon the heart.
There is neither ignorance nor attainment;
phenomena are fundamentally not non-existent.
Wisdom is difficult to measure.
With a joyful mind free from defilement,
light is emitted that fills the ten directions;
the stage Difficult to Conquer appears before one.
The Great Site of Enlightenment for Far-reaching Travel;
immovable, he transcends to the other shore;
the King of Dharma through Excellent Wisdom.
Because there is nothing to be attained,
the essence of quiescent extinction is unattainable;
true emptiness transcends the reach of the hand.
Originally devoid of form or appearance,
the three types of giving are provisionally established;
through the four wisdoms, the Dharma and its metaphors are revealed.
The six perfections are called the universal gate;
the ten stages and the teachings of the Three Vehicles are difficult for all sages to fathom.
A Bodhisattva is truly difficult for those on the Buddha-way to recognize;
a sattva is but an ordinary person.
Sentient beings must realize their true nature;
revere the Buddha and do not let your mind be solitary.
He is the spiritual friend of the world.
The dharmas of speech are subtle or coarse;
the mind of sudden awakening is equanimous.
In the interim, there are signs to be eliminated.
"By relying on the Prajñāpāramitā. *Prajñā* means wisdom;
*pāra* means that which has no basis.
The mind is vast emptiness;
internally and externally, all is unconditioned.
Its nature is empty, possessing unimpeded eloquence.
Those who have mastered the three realms are rare;
they perceive the Great Vision and clarify the Great Dharma,
all praising its inconceivability.
The mind is without obstruction;
liberated, the mind is unimpeded,
as vast as empty space.
In the four intermediate directions there is not a single thing;
above and below are entirely the same.
In coming and going, the mind is autonomous.
The person and the dharma do not meet;
seeking the Way, one sees no object.
Moving spontaneously, one emerges from the cage of affliction.
Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear.
The mind of birth and death is fearful;
the unconditioned nature is inherently at peace.
When objects are forgotten, the mind also ceases;
the ocean of nature is serene and vast.
The three bodies return to the pure land.
The eight consciousnesses depart from causes and conditions;
the six supernormal powers accord with the true mark.
Returning to the fundamental, one reverts to the source.
Far removed from all inverted dreams and delusions,
do not establish either of the two extremes;
do not even mentally cultivate the Middle Way.
When one perceives the nature, birth and death are exhausted;
there is nothing to be sought in bodhi.
To seek the true Buddha outside of oneself—
When perversion ceases for a lifetime,
sitting in stillness brings peace and joy to the body;
the fruit of non-action is naturally complete.
Ultimate nirvana; ultimate non-arising nature; purity is nirvana.
Ordinary beings cannot fathom the Sage;
until one has arrived there, it must necessarily be difficult.
Those still in training (śaikṣa) are yet beyond learning (aśaikṣa).
The Buddha’s wisdom grows ever deeper and more profound;
one must ultimately realize the principle of the mind's non-existence.
Do not cling to the source of the stilled mind.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time:
those of the past do not speak of reality;
those of the future do not constitute truth.
Now, with the Bodhi-seeds,
the Dharma is named the Mysterious Gate;
the three bodies converge into one.
The single nature universally encompasses all bodies;
realizing this principle, one transcends the three periods of time. Through this single dharma, one attains the state of causelessness.
By relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha’s wisdom is profound and difficult to fathom;
his insight and understanding are vast and boundless.
The unsurpassed mind is perfectly pervasive;
the light of compassion fills the great trichiliocosm.
Within the heart of quiescent extinction, there is skillful means.
Establishing more than ten thousand methods,
the Bodhisattva employs many skillful means to universally save those among humans and devas.
Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra.
With prajñā as the divine mantra,
one is able to eliminate doubts regarding the five aggregates.
All afflictions are completely severed;
purity arises through separation.
The four wisdoms are as boundless as the waves.
The eight consciousnesses possess divine power;
the lamp of the mind illuminates the Dharma-realm.
This very state is bodhi.
This is the unsurpassed mantra;
unsurpassed and most excellent,
it delivers all who are deluded.
O Mahā, Lord of the Three Realms!
We pray that you extensively give rise to compassion,
being able to accord with the intentions of all sentient beings.
Following the stream, they guide and transform the deluded;
person after person is led to the other shore.
This is achieved through me, not through them.
This is the peerless mantra;
it completes the Buddha-way for the thousand sages.
Its dharma-power is unsurpassed.
True emptiness extinguishes all existence;
it manifests many transformation bodies to come for the sake of the suffering of sentient beings.
Having departed, you have become the Mara of the world;
even the kalpa-stones shall all come to an end,
yet I alone remain in this Sahā world.
It can eliminate all suffering; it is true and not false.
May the Buddha’s compassionate heart be vast, delivering sentient beings in every lifetime.
Hōnen expounded the True Dharma and universally exhorted all to practice with urgency;
by turning the mind, one perceives the true aspect of reality.
Seeing the end of suffering, one realizes non-arising;
the three evil realms are forever stilled.
Within this vast and open bliss, there is joy at every turn.
Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā mantra is spoken;
therefore, the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) is spoken.
Those who have not yet awakened should quickly turn their minds [toward it].
The six thieves and the ten evils are extinguished;
the mountain of Māra is crushed to its very base.
This divine mantra eliminates the three poisons.
The flower of the mind blooms in five petals;
the fruit ripens and the roots intertwine.
At every step, one beholds the Tathāgata.
Then he spoke the mantra: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*. *Gate* is the fundamental pillar of the school;
it supports the pivot and erects the banner of the Dharma.
The Tathāgata is most honored and supreme;
do not attempt to measure his mind with ordinary thoughts.
He is without limit and without middle boundary.
Neither short nor long is the Prajñāpāramitā;
it remains constant throughout all ages, past and present.
The Heart Sutra of the Great Perfection of Wisdom. 2.
Treatise on the Destruction of Characteristics, Second Section: Treatise on the Destruction of Characteristics. Question:
Suppose there is a person who...
One who aspires to seek the Buddha-way:
what dharma should they cultivate that is most concise and essential?
The answer is:
One contemplates only the single dharma of the mind,
which comprehensively subsumes all dharmas.
This is the most concise and essential [teaching]. It is asked:
"What single dharma is able to encompass all dharmas?"
Answer: The mind is the root of the myriad dharmas;
all phenomena are produced solely by the mind.
If one can thoroughly understand the mind,
then all phenomena are fully present,
just as a great tree possesses all its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
All things arise depending upon their roots;
likewise, if one cuts down a tree and removes its root, it will inevitably die.
If one understands the mind and cultivates the Way, [the same principle applies].
Thus, one conserves effort and achieves success with ease; whereas,
if one cultivates the path without understanding the mind,
one expends labor to no avail.
Therefore, know that all good and evil arise from one's own mind;
to seek them elsewhere apart from the mind is ultimately impossible.
Question:
How is it that observing the mind is designated as "understanding"? Answer:
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom,
they realize that the four great elements and the five aggregates are fundamentally empty and without self.
One clearly perceives that the arising of the mind's activity has two kinds of distinctions. What are these two?
The first is the pure mind.
Second is the defiled mind.
These two types of mind are naturally present within the dharma-realm;
they have been coexistent from the very beginning.
Although detached from provisional conditions,
they remain mutually dependent;
with a pure mind, one constantly delights in wholesome causes.
The essence of defilement constantly contemplates evil karma;
if one does not undergo what is defiled,
then one is called a noble one (ārya).
Thus, one is able to remain far removed from all suffering and realize the bliss of nirvana. However,
if one creates karma following a defiled mind, [the result will be otherwise].
Being shrouded and enveloped by these fetters is what defines one as an ordinary person; thus,
they sink and wander within the three realms.
They undergo various kinds of suffering. Why is this?
Because that defiled mind obstructs the essence of True Suchness (tathatā).
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:
"Within the bodies of sentient beings,
there exists the vajra-buddha-nature."
It is like the orb of the sun, its essence luminous, perfect, vast, and boundless;
yet because it is shrouded by the heavy clouds of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*),
it cannot manifest, just as the light of a lamp inside a jar cannot be seen.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; it is because they are shrouded by ignorance [that it is not manifest]."
One cannot attain liberation.
Buddha-nature is precisely the nature of awakening;
it simply consists in awakening oneself and awakening others.
When awakening-wisdom is clear and lucid,
it is called liberation; therefore,
one knows that all wholesome qualities have awakening as their root.
By means of that faculty of awakening,
one is thus able to manifest the trees of all virtues and the fruit of nirvana.
It is through this that it is accomplished.
Observing the mind in this manner may be called "understanding."
Question:
It was stated above that true suchness, buddha-nature, and all merits have awakening as their root.
I do not yet understand what the mind of ignorance takes as its root.
Answer:
Although the mind of ignorance possesses eighty-four thousand afflictions and sensual desires, as well as evils as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
All are caused by the three poisons,
which serve as their root.
As for these three poisons:
These are precisely greed, hatred, and delusion.
These three poisons of the mind are themselves fully capable of encompassing all manner of evils.
It is like a great tree:
although its root is one,
the branches and leaves it produces are infinite in number.
From each of those three roots of poison,
all manner of evil karmas arise.
It exceeds the former by hundreds of thousands of millions of times;
it is beyond all comparison.
In this way, the mind of the three poisons manifests as the six sense organs within its original substance.
They are also called the six thieves;
that is, the six consciousnesses.
It is because these six consciousnesses enter and exit through the various sense organs.
Clinging greedily to the myriad objects of the senses can produce evil karma and obstruct the essence of True Suchness.
Therefore, they are called the "six thieves.
Sentient beings are deluded and disturbed in body and mind by these three poisons and six thieves.
Sinking into birth and death,
they transmigrate through the six realms,
undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction.
It is like a great river that,
due to a small source,
maintains an unceasing flow of trickling water.
Thus it is able to overflow and spread,
its waves and surges extending for ten thousand *li*.
Yet, if there were another person who were to cut off its source, [the flow would cease].
Then all currents will cease.
Those who seek liberation can transform the three poisons into the three clusters of pure precepts.
Transforming the six thieves into the six pāramitās,
one naturally and eternally leaves behind the ocean of all suffering.
Question:
The six realms of existence and the three worlds are vast and boundless;
if one observes only the mind alone,
by what means can one escape from endless suffering?
Answer: The karmic retributions of the three realms are produced solely by the mind.
Fundamentally, if there were no mind, [they would not exist].
Within the triple world,
one immediately transcends the triple world. As for that triple world:
These are the three poisons.
Greed constitutes the desire realm;
hatred constitutes the form realm.
Delusion constitutes the formless realm;
thus they are called the three realms. It is by means of these three poisons [that they are so designated].
The lightness or heaviness of the karma created results in different retributions,
leading beings to their respective destinations among the six realms.
Therefore, they are called the six destinies (*ṣadgati*). Question:
How are they divided into six according to their lightness and heaviness?
Answer: Sentient beings do not understand the true cause;
with deluded minds, they practice wholesome deeds.
One cannot avoid being born within the three lower realms of the triple world.
What are these three lower realms?
This refers to those who, deluded in their cultivation of the ten wholesome paths,
falsely seek happiness yet remain unable to escape the realm of craving.
Born into the heavenly realms,
they remain deluded regarding the observance of the five precepts and give rise to false attachments and aversions.
Unable to avoid the realm of anger,
they are born into the human realm,
where they remain deludedly attached to conditioned phenomena.
Believing in false teachings while seeking merit,
they remain unable to escape the realm of delusion and are reborn in the asura realm.
These three types are called the three light destinies.
What are the three heavy destinies?
That is to say, by indulging the three poisons of the mind,
one creates only evil karma and falls into the three lower realms.
If the karma of greed is heavy,
one falls into the realm of hungry ghosts;
if the karma of anger is heavy, [one falls into the realm of hell].
Those whose karma of delusion is heavy fall into the realm of animals.
Thus, with these three levels combined with the preceding three light [degrees],
they constitute the six destinies (ṣadgati).
Thus, one knows that all suffering and karma arise from the mind itself;
by simply being able to collect the mind,
one becomes free from all evils.
The suffering of saṃsāra within the three realms and six destinies will naturally be extinguished,
and one will immediately attain liberation.
Question:
As the Buddha has said,
"For three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas..."
"Having undergone immeasurable toil and suffering,
one finally attains the Buddha-way.
Why do you now say that merely contemplating the mind and subduing the three poisons is itself called liberation?"
Answer: That which the Buddha has spoken contains no falsehood.
The term "asaṃkhyeya kalpas" refers to the mind of the three poisons;
in the language of the Hu, it is called "asaṃkhyeya."
The names of these [afflictions] in the Han language are incalculable.
Within this mind of the three poisons,
there are as many evil thoughts as there are sands in the Ganges.
Within each and every thought-moment,
it is as if one kalpa has passed;
thus, they are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, beyond counting.
Therefore, it is said that there are three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
for the nature of true suchness has been covered over by the three poisons.
If one does not transcend those three great poisons of the mind, as numerous as the sands of three *gaṅgā* rivers,
how can this be called liberation? Now,
if one is able to transform the three poisons of the mind— greed, hatred, and delusion— [then it is liberation].
This constitutes the three liberations;
this is what is called attaining transcendence across the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas. For sentient beings of the末法 (mofa / final dharma) age, [this is the path].
Being foolish and of dull faculties,
they do not understand the Tathāgata’s teaching on the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas as a secret doctrine;
consequently, they claim that it takes aeons of dust to achieve Buddhahood.
"Would this not cause confusion for practitioners and cause them to retreat from the path to bodhi?
[The interlocutor] asked: "O Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva..."
By upholding the three clusters of pure precepts and practicing the six pāramitās,
one will finally attain the Buddha-way.
If you now command students to observe only the mind and not cultivate ethical conduct,
how can they become Buddhas?
Answer: The three clusters of pure precepts (tri-śīkṣāpada) are precisely the restraint of the mind of the three poisons.
By subduing the three poisons of the mind, one accomplishes an immeasurable accumulation of goodness.
"Accumulation" means a gathering;
immeasurable wholesome dharmas are universally gathered within the mind.
Therefore, it is called the Threefold Pure Precepts.
As for the six pāramitās, they are precisely the purification of the six sense faculties.
In the language of the Hu, it is called *pāramitā*;
in the language of Han, it is called "reaching the other shore.
This means that because the six sense organs are pure, they are not defiled by the six sensory objects.
This refers to crossing the river of afflictions and reaching the shore of bodhi;
therefore, they are called the six pāramitās.
Question:
As stated in the sutras,
what are the three clusters of pure precepts?
I vow to sever all evil.
I vow to cultivate all goodness.
I vow to deliver all sentient beings.
Now, you say that this only speaks of restraining the three poisons of the mind;
does this not contradict the meaning of the text? Answer:
The sūtras spoken by the Buddha are words of truth.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva was practicing during past causal conditions, [he attained this].
To counteract the three poisons,
one should give rise to three vows to sever all evil.
Therefore, one should constantly maintain the precepts;
regarding the poison of greed,
one vows to cultivate all that is wholesome.
Therefore, one should constantly practice meditative concentration.
Facing the poison of anger,
one vows to deliver all sentient beings.
Therefore, one constantly cultivates wisdom as an antidote to the poison of delusion;
this is because one upholds these three kinds of pure dharmas: ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
One is able to transcend those three poisons and attain the Buddha-way;
when all evils are extinguished,
this is called "severance."
The complete possession of all virtues is called cultivation;
for it is by means of this that one can sever evil and cultivate goodness.
Then all practices will be perfected;
self and others will both benefit,
and all sentient beings will be universally rescued.
This is called "crossing over.
Therefore, one should know that the precepts one cultivates are not separate from the mind;
if one's own mind is pure, [the precepts are likewise pure].
Consequently, all Buddha-lands are entirely pure.
Thus, a sutra says:
"When the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled."
When the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure.
If you wish to attain a pure land,
you should purify your own mind.
According to the purity of one's mind, so too is the Buddha-land pure;
the three clusters of pure precepts are spontaneously accomplished.
Question:
As stated in the sūtras,
the six pāramitās are also called the six perfections (ṣaḍ-pāramitā).
That which is called generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration,
and wisdom— what is now referred to as the purification of the six sense faculties is termed "pāramitā."
What is meant by "comprehensive integration"?
Furthermore, what is the meaning of the six perfections?
Answer: If one wishes to cultivate the six perfections,
one should purify the six sense faculties and subdue the six thieves.
To be able to abandon the thief of the eye and remain detached from all objects of form is called generosity.
One is able to restrain the thief of the ear;
regarding the sensory object of sound,
one does not allow it to become heedless.
This is called upholding the precepts;
it can subdue the thief of the nose and treat all fragrances and stenches as equal.
Mastery and gentleness are called patience;
it is able to subdue the thief of the tongue.
Not craving various flavors,
but praising, chanting, and expounding [the Dharma], is called diligence.
He is able to subdue the thieves of the body;
amidst all sensory contacts and desires,
he remains serene and unmoving.
This is called meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);
it can subdue the thief of the mind and does not follow ignorance.
Constantly cultivating awakened wisdom is called "wisdom. As for the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*),
they are "transports" (or conveyances).
The six pāramitās are like a boat or raft that can transport sentient beings and enable them to reach the other shore.
Therefore, they are called the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā). Question:
The Sūtra says:
When Śākyamuni Tathāgata was a bodhisattva,
he once drank three dou and six sheng of milk gruel before attaining the Way of Buddhahood.
Having first drunk milk and later realized the fruit of Buddhahood—
how could this be achieved through the mere contemplation of the mind to attain liberation?
He replied,
"I truly know that what you say is not false;
it must have been due to consuming milk."
Only then does one become a Buddha.
Regarding the statement that he "consumed milk," there are two types.
As for that which was consumed by the Buddha:
This is not the impure milk of the world;
rather, it is the pure Dharma-milk of True Suchness (Tathatā).
As for the "three pecks":
These are the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣāpada*).
"Six pints" refers to the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
When attaining the path of Buddhahood,
it is by consuming such pure milk of the Dharma that one finally realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
If one were to say that the Tathāgata consumes the impure, mixed, and foul-smelling milk of cows from this world,
would that not be an extreme instance of slander and delusion?
As for True Suchness (Tathatā):
From this point on, it is the indestructible vajra,
the untainted dharmakāya,
forever free from all worldly sufferings.
Why must one satisfy hunger and thirst with such impure milk?
As it is said in the sutras:
That ox does not stay on high plateaus,
nor in low-lying damp places;
it does not eat parched grain, chaff, or bran.
It does not graze in the same herd as ordinary oxen.
This ox’s body is the color of purple-polished gold. As for this ox:
This is Vairocana Buddha.
With great compassion,
he takes pity on all beings.
Therefore, from within the essence of the pure Dharma,
there issues forth the subtle milk of the Dharma— the three clusters of pure precepts and the six pāramitās—
to nourish all who seek liberation.
Such a truly pure cow and its pure milk are not only what the Tathāgata drank to achieve enlightenment.
If all sentient beings are able to drink it,
they shall all attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Question:
As stated in the sūtras,
the Buddha commanded sentient beings to construct monasteries and cast or carve images.
Burn incense and scatter flowers;
light perpetual lamps throughout the six periods of the day and night.
Circumambulating stupas while walking in meditation,
observing the fast, and performing prostrations—
these various meritorious deeds.
All shall attain the Buddha-way.
If one contemplates only the mind,
it comprehensively encompasses all practices.
To say such a thing would be false. [The opponent] replies:
The sūtras spoken by the Buddha contain immeasurable skillful means,
because all sentient beings possess dull faculties and limited capacities.
Failing to realize the profound meaning,
one uses conditioned phenomena as a metaphor for the unconditioned; yet,
if one does not further cultivate internal practice, [the goal remains unattained].
To seek only outwardly,
hoping thereby to obtain blessings—
such a thing is impossible.
The term "ārāma" is a word from the Western regions;
in this land, it is translated as "pure ground."
If one eternally eliminates the three poisons and constantly purifies the six sense faculties,
body and mind will become profoundly serene.
To purify both the interior and exterior is what is called constructing a monastery;
to cast and fashion images is likewise so defined.
This is precisely all sentient beings seeking the Buddha-way;
that is to say, they cultivate various practices of awakening and emulate the true countenance and wondrous marks of the Tathāgata.
How could this be something fashioned by casting or engraving gold and copper?
Therefore, those who seek liberation take the body as the furnace.
Taking the Dharma as fire,
taking wisdom as the skilled craftsman,
and taking the three clusters of pure precepts and the six pāramitās as the mold and the frame.
Smelt and refine the *tathāgatagarbha* (Buddha-nature) within one's own body,
causing it to enter entirely into the molds of all precepts,
and practice according to the teachings.
Without any deficiency or flaw,
it spontaneously accomplishes the image of the true countenance;
that is to say, the ultimately eternal and subtle form-body (*rūpakāya*).
It is not a conditioned phenomenon subject to decay.
If a person seeks the Way,
they must understand how to thus cast and fashion this true likeness.
On what basis do you speak so lightly of merit?
Furthermore, as for burning incense,
it is not the kind of incense characterized by worldly forms.
This is indeed the fragrance of the unconditioned True Dharma;
it permeates all foul odors, ignorance, and evil karma,
causing them all to be utterly extinguished.
Regarding the fragrance of the True Dharma,
there are five kinds.
The first is the fragrance of ethical discipline.
That which is called the ability to sever all evils and the ability to cultivate all virtues;
second, the fragrance of meditative concentration.
The so-called deep faith in the Mahāyāna with a mind that never regresses;
third, the fragrance of wisdom.
That which is called the fourth, the fragrance of liberation, consists of constantly observing within one's own body and mind.
It is that which can sever all fetters of ignorance.
Fifth is the fragrance of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
it is the constant illumination of contemplative observation.
Pervading everywhere without obstruction—
these five kinds of incense are called the most supreme of fragrances.
Incomparable in the world;
while the Buddha was in the world,
he caused his disciples to...
With the fire of wisdom,
one burns such priceless precious incense to make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
In the present age, sentient beings do not understand the true meaning of the Tathāgata;
they merely use external fire to burn worldly aloeswood and sandalwood.
How can one obtain the hoped-for karmic rewards from the fragrant incense of frankincense,
which is a material obstruction?
Furthermore, the meaning of scattering flowers is likewise so:
it refers to the preaching of the True Dharma.
The flowers of all virtues benefit sentient beings,
scattering and moistening all.
Upon the nature of suchness,
this flower of merit universally bestows adornment.
Praised by the Buddha,
it is ultimately eternal and abiding,
with no time of decay or fall.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who scatters such flowers,
they shall obtain immeasurable merit.
If one says that the Tathāgata causes sentient beings to cut and trim silken fabrics,
or to injure and damage plants and trees.
To think that they are scattered flowers— this is impossible. Why is this so?
One who upholds the pure precepts does not allow themselves to transgress against the myriad phenomena of all heavens and earths.
If one incurs a grave offense even through a transgression committed by mistake,
how much more so now for intentionally violating the pure precepts and harming all living beings?
Seeking a reward of merit,
one desires to benefit others but instead causes harm;
how could such a thing possibly exist?
The "long-burning lamp" is the mind of perfect enlightenment;
it is the clarity of awakening.
It is likened to a lamp;
therefore, for all who seek liberation,
the body serves as the lamp-stand.
The mind is the wick of the lamp;
increasing various virtuous conducts serves as the addition of oil.
Wisdom is clear and penetrating;
it is like a lamp that burns constantly.
Such is the lamp of true awakening.
It illuminates all the darkness of ignorance and delusion;
by means of this wheel of Dharma,
it can sequentially reveal and demonstrate [the truth].
This is like one lamp lighting hundreds of thousands of lamps;
as the lamps continue to light one another without end,
it is called "Perpetual Illumination."
In the past, there was a Buddha named Dīpaṃkara;
the meaning is likewise the same.
Ignorant sentient beings do not understand the Tathāgata’s teaching of skillful means;
they practice exclusively in falsehood.
Clinging to the conditioned,
he then lit a lamp of ghee and oil in the world to illuminate an empty room.
To then claim that this accords with the teachings—
is this not erroneous? Why is this so?
The Buddha emits a ray of light from a single hair-tuft between his eyebrows that can illuminate eighteen thousand worlds;
how could it possibly be like such a lamp of ghee and oil?
Considering this as beneficial,
one should examine this principle: is it not indeed so?
Furthermore, regarding those who practice the Way during the six periods:
this refers to all times within the six sense faculties.
Constantly practicing the Buddha-way,
cultivating all practices of awakening,
and subduing the six sense faculties.
Not abandoning [the practice] for a long duration is called "practicing the path during the six periods.
As for those who circumambulate the stupa while practicing the path:
The stupa is the body. One should cultivate the practice of awakening by circumambulating the body and mind,
with every thought-moment uninterrupted.
This is called circumambulating the stupa.
All the sages of the past practiced this path until the time of their parinirvāṇa.
At present, people of the world do not understand this principle;
they have never practiced it internally,
but only cling to seeking it externally.
Taking their physical, obstructive bodies,
they run and gallop day and night around the stupas of the world.
One merely exhausts oneself,
deriving no benefit whatsoever for true nature.
Furthermore, those who observe the fast must understand the underlying meaning; if they do not grasp this principle,
[the practice will be in vain].
It is merely empty labor.
"Zhai" (fasting) means "to align";
it refers to what is called aligning and rectifying the body and mind.
It does not allow for distraction;
"holding" means guarding,
specifically regarding all precepts and practices.
To maintain this in accordance with the Dharma,
one must externally restrain the six sense faculties and internally subdue the three poisons.
Diligently observing and purifying body and mind,
and realizing this meaning,
is called upholding the fast.
There are five kinds of food.
The first is the food of dharma-delight,
which refers to relying upon and upholding the True Dharma.
They joyfully receive and practice it.
Second is the food of dhyāna-delight,
which consists of inner and outer tranquility and stillness.
The body and mind are joyful and at ease.
Third is mindfulness of food,
which means constantly being mindful of all Buddhas.
The fourth is the vow of eating with mind and speech in accord,
which means [to maintain this intention] whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
Fifth is the food of liberation, which means that the mind is always pure.
Untainted by worldly dust—
these five kinds of food are called observing the fast.
Furthermore, if there is another person...
To refrain from eating these five kinds of pure food while claiming to observe the fast—
such a thing is impossible.
To merely sever the nutriment of ignorance and immediately form a conceptual understanding is called breaking the fast.
If there is also destruction,
how can one obtain merit?
There are those in the world who are deluded.
Failing to realize this principle,
one’s body and mind become negligent, leading entirely to various evils;
one indulges in greed and lusts according to one's whims.
Feeling no shame or remorse,
he merely abstained from external food,
observing the fast for his own sake.
This is certainly impossible.
Furthermore, one who performs prostrations should do so in accordance with the Dharma.
One must internally realize the principle of luminosity (prabhāsvara),
while externally adapting to circumstances through skillful means;
one should thus comprehend this meaning.
This is what is called "acting in accordance with the Dharma.
Now, ritual (*li*) is reverence;
bowing (*bai*) is prostration.
What is called revering true nature and subduing ignorance is termed "prostration."
If one can forever extinguish evil thoughts and constantly maintain wholesome mindfulness,
then even though one does not attend to signs, [the result will follow].
This is called prostration;
its characteristic is precisely the characteristic of dharmas.
The World-Honored One intended to cause worldly people to manifest a humble and submissive mind.
It is also for the purpose of prostration;
therefore, one must bend the outer body to demonstrate inner reverence.
Awakening to the external as luminous within,
such that nature and characteristics are in accord;
yet if one does not further practice according to the principles of the Dharma.
They cling solely to seeking externally;
internally, they indulge in greed and delusion,
constantly committing evil deeds.
Externally, they vainly exhaust their physical forms,
falsely manifesting dignified deportment while lacking any sense of shame before the sages.
They merely deceive ordinary people;
they cannot escape saṃsāra,
so how could they achieve merit and virtue?
Question:
As it is said in the sutras,
"Recall the Buddha with a sincere mind."
One will certainly attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land;
by means of this single gateway,
one shall immediately become a Buddha.
Question: Why rely on the contemplation of the mind to seek liberation? Answer:
Now, those who practice the recollection of the Buddha must maintain right mindfulness;
the definitive meaning constitutes what is correct.
If one’s understanding is not definitive, it is erroneous;
through right mindfulness, one will certainly attain rebirth there.
How could one with erroneous mindfulness reach that place?
"Buddha" means awakening.
It refers to being aware of one's body and mind so as not to allow evil to arise.
"Mindfulness" means recollection;
that is to say, it is the recollection and maintenance of ethical conduct and the non-forgetfulness of diligence.
To thoroughly comprehend such meanings is called mindfulness; therefore,
one knows that mindfulness resides in the mind.
It does not reside in words.
One uses the trap to seek the fish;
once the fish is caught, one forgets the trap.
One seeks the meaning through words;
having grasped the meaning, one forgets the words.
Since one has invoked the name of the Buddha, [the goal is attained].
One must know that in the way of nianfo,
if the mind lacks sincerity and the mouth recites empty names, it is in vain.
The three poisons surge from within;
the notions of self and other fill the breast.
With this mind of ignorance...
To seek the Buddha outwardly is to labor in vain; consider, for instance,
the difference between reciting and mindful contemplation.
The principles differ significantly:
that which is on the lips is called recitation;
that which is in the mind is called mindfulness.
Therefore, one should know that mindfulness arises from the mind;
it is called the gateway of awakening practice.
To recite it with the mouth is merely to chant it aloud.
This is merely the characteristic of sound.
To grasp at external phenomena in search of the principle is ultimately impossible.
Therefore, we know that the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha cultivated by all the sages of the past was in no way an external teaching;
it was solely an investigation into the inner mind.
The mind is the source of all goodness;
the mind is the sovereign of all virtues.
Nirvana is eternal bliss.
It arises from the true mind;
the cycle of the three realms also originates from the mind.
The mind is the gateway to transcendence.
The mind is the gateway to liberation.
For one who knows the entrance, how could they worry about not being able to enter?
For one who recognizes the gateway, why should they fear it will not be passed through?
Question:
As stated in the *Jentākasūtra*,
one bathes the assembly of monks.
One obtains immeasurable merit;
this depends upon the phenomena of the ritual act,
whereby merit is first accomplished.
If one asks whether this is compatible with the contemplation of the mind,
the answer is:
"As for those who bathe the assembly of monks."
This is not a mundane, conditioned matter.
The World-Honored One once preached the Jentāka-sūtra for his disciples.
Desiring to cause them to receive and uphold the method of ritual bathing,
that warm chamber was none other than his own body.
Therefore, one kindles the fire of wisdom and heats the bathwater of pure precepts to bathe the *tathāgatagarbha*—
the Buddha-nature— within one's body.
He upholds and practices seven dharmas as his own adornment;
on that day, the bhikṣu is of keen intelligence and superior wisdom.
They all realized the Sage’s intention and practiced according to his instructions,
thereby accomplishing merit.
They both ascended to the fruits of sainthood.
Beings of the present age cannot fathom this matter;
they take it to be worldly water.
To claim that washing away physical obstructions is based on the sutras—
is this not an error?
Furthermore, true suchness and buddha-nature are not ordinary forms, afflictions, or defilements;
they are fundamentally without marks.
How could one possibly wash an unconditioned body with obstructive water?
This is inconsistent with the facts;
how then can one awaken to the Way?
If one desires for the body to attain purity,
one should contemplate this body as having originally arisen from the impurity of craving and desire.
Foul and filthy, it is crowded and packed,
filling both the interior and exterior;
if one seeks purity by washing this body, [it will never be found].
It is like washing a moat;
only when the moat is completely emptied does it become clean.
By this one may verify it.
It is clearly known that washing the exterior is not the teaching of the Buddha.
Therefore, worldly affairs are employed as metaphors for the True Doctrine.
The merits of making offerings through seven matters are explained in secret.
There are seven such matters. What are these seven?
First, pure water;
second, kindled fire;
third, cleansing powder.
Fourth, tooth-sticks;
fifth, pure ashes; sixth, ghee.
Seventh is the undergarment.
These seven items are used as metaphors for seven dharmas.
By means of these seven dharmas, all sentient beings bathe and adorn themselves,
thereby able to eliminate the poisonous mind and the defilements of ignorance.
As for those seven dharmas:
the first is pure precepts,
which wash away transgressions and faults.
First, it is like pure water that washes away all dust and defilements;
second, it is wisdom that observes both the internal and the external.
It is like kindling a fire to warm pure water.
Third is discernment:
the deliberate rejection of all evils.
It is like cleansing soap that can purify dirt and grease;
fourth is reality,
which severs all delusive thoughts.
Just as a willow twig can eliminate bad breath,
the fifth is right faith,
which is resolute and free from doubt.
It is like pure ash rubbed upon the body to ward off wind.
Sixth is gentleness: enduring and willingly accepting [insults].
It is like medicinal oil that permeates and moistens the skin.
Seventh is shame and remorse,
which involve repenting for all evil karmas.
Just as undergarments conceal an unattractive body,
the aforementioned seven dharmas are the esoteric meanings within the sūtras;
they are all taught for the sake of those with sharp faculties in the Mahāyāna.
This is not for the sake of those of meager wisdom or inferior, ordinary persons;
this is why people of the present age are unable to understand or realize it.
I have observed that those of shallow learning nowadays—
They know only to take the outward appearance of things as their achievement;
they squander vast amounts of wealth and treasure,
causing great injury to creatures both aquatic and terrestrial.
They vainly construct images and stupas,
pointlessly conscripting laborers to pile up wood and stack mud.
He planned and painted the design with focused devotion and all his strength,
sacrificing himself for the sake of others.
Having not yet understood shame and remorse,
when have they ever awakened?
Seeing conditioned phenomena, they are constantly and diligently attached to them.
To speak of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) would leave one dazed as if lost;
moreover, by craving the minor compassion of the present life,
how can one perceive the great suffering of the future?
This practice of cultivation is merely a waste of effort;
it turns one's back on the correct path and leads toward the heterodox.
Who says that one obtains blessings?
It is simply by being able to collect the mind for inward illumination and through clear observation of the external.
Cutting off the three poisons so they may forever perish;
closing the gates of the six thieves so they cannot invade or disturb;
thus, the merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges arise spontaneously.
Various adornments and innumerable dharma-gates are each and every one fully accomplished.
Transcending the mundane to realize the sacred—
this direct witnessing is not far off;
awakening occurs in an instant.
Why trouble yourself with white hair?
The gate of truth is profound and secret;
how could it ever be fully described?
A brief exposition on the contemplation of the mind is presented, describing only a small portion thereof.
Thus, a verse is spoken:
In the beginning, I sought the mind, yet the mind held itself fast; Seeking the mind, I could not find it, waiting instead for the mind to know itself.
The Buddha-nature is not found outside of the mind; When the mind arises, it is precisely at that moment that transgression arises.
I originally sought the mind and did not seek a Buddha; I came to realize that the three realms are empty and devoid of substance.
If you wish to seek the Buddha, seek only the mind; this very mind, mind after mind, is the Buddha.
*End of Chapter 3: Refuting Characteristics*. **Chapter 4: Two Kinds of Entry** Now, there are many paths for entering the Way.
To summarize, these do not exceed two types:
the first is entry by means of principle.
The second is entry by practice.
As for entry by principle,
it means awakening to the fundamental tenet by relying on the teachings.
With deep faith, one realizes that all living beings share the same true nature,
yet it remains unmanifested because it is shrouded by adventitious defilements and deluded thoughts.
If one abandons delusion to return to the truth,
remaining concentrated in the "wall-contemplation," there is neither self nor other.
Ordinary beings and sages are equal and one;
they abide firmly without wavering,
no longer following the teachings of words and texts.
This is precisely in accord with ultimate principle;
it is free from discrimination,
tranquil, and unconditioned.
This is called entry by principle.
As for entry by practice,
it refers to the four practices.
All other practices are entirely included within these.
What are the four? First, the practice of repaying grievances.
Second, practice in accordance with conditions;
third, practice free from seeking;
fourth, practice in conformity with the Dharma.
What is the practice of requiting grievances?
It means that when a practitioner of the Path undergoes suffering, they should reflect to themselves: "Throughout countless kalpas from the past, I..."
Abandoning the fundamental and following the derivative, they wander through the various realms of existence,
frequently giving rise to resentment and hatred,
and inflicting infinite harm and injury.
Although there is no offense now,
these are all the ripening fruits of past calamities and evil karma.
Neither gods nor humans can see it; one accepts it with a willing heart and endures it,
without any resentment or complaint.
The Sūtra says:
"When encountering suffering, one does not grieve. Why is this?
Because of thorough understanding,
when this mind arises,
it accords with principle.
Because one advances on the Path by taking grievances as the substance [of practice],
it is called the "practice of repaying grievances.
Second is the "practice that accords with conditions."
Sentient beings are without self;
they are all driven by the conditions of karma,
experiencing both suffering and pleasure equally.
All things arise from conditions.
If one obtains superior retributions such as honor and renown,
these are the results induced by past causes from a previous existence.
Now I have finally obtained it;
yet when conditions are exhausted, it returns to nothingness.
What cause for joy is there?
Gain and loss follow conditions;
the mind neither increases nor decreases.
It is unmoved by the winds of joy.
It is in profound accord with the Way;
therefore, it is said that one acts in accordance with conditions.
Third is the practitioner who seeks nothing.
The people of the world are long deluded;
they greedily cling everywhere,
which is called "seeking."
The wise realize the truth;
its principle runs contrary to the mundane.
They settle their minds in non-action.
Form follows the turning of conditions;
all phenomena are thus empty.
There is nothing to be desired or delighted in.
Merit and darkness constantly follow one another;
dwelling long within the three realms is like being inside a burning house.
All who possess a body experience suffering; who can find peace?
One must thoroughly comprehend this truth.
Therefore, one abandons all states of existence,
ceases conceptualization, and remains without seeking.
As the Sūtra says:
All seeking is suffering;
the absence of seeking is bliss.
To discern and know that the absence of seeking is the true practice of the Way.
Therefore, it is said that there is no practice of seeking.
Fourth, regarding "practice in accordance with the Dharma":
the principle of intrinsic purity is designated as the Dharma.
Believing and understanding this principle,
all characteristics are empty;
there is neither defilement nor attachment.
There is neither this nor that.
As the Sūtra says:
"In dharmas there are no sentient beings."
Because it is free from the defilement of sentient beings,
the Dharma is without self; because it is free from the defilement of self, [it is without self].
If a wise person can believe and understand this principle,
they should act in accordance with the Dharma;
for the essence of the Dharma is free from stinginess.
They practice the giving of body, life, and wealth as acts of charity,
their minds free from any sense of regret or stinginess, and they have attained a thorough understanding of the three kinds of emptiness.
Neither leaning nor clinging,
he acts solely to remove defilements and to transform sentient beings according to their needs.
Yet one does not grasp at signs;
this constitutes one's own practice and is further able to benefit others.
It can also adorn the path to enlightenment.
As it is with the practice of giving (*dāna*),
so it is with the other five perfections as well.
To eliminate deluded thoughts,
one practices the six perfections while remaining without any [subjective] practice.
This is called practicing in accordance with the Dharma. A verse says:
Externally ceasing all conditions, Internally the mind is without panting; The mind is like a wall.
One may thereby enter the Way and clarify the Heart-Essence of the Buddha;
when practice and understanding correspond without error, one is called an Ancestor.

[End of Section 2: The Two Kinds of Entry] Section Four: The Dharma-Gate of Settling the Mind. The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) and the *Zhengfayan zang* (Treasury of the True Dharma Eye) record that when people are deluded, they pursue phenomena.
When one understands, the dharmas follow the person;
when one understands, consciousness subsumes form.
When one is deluded, form subsumes consciousness.
However, all mental discrimination and calculation,
as well as whatever is directly perceived by oneself, are entirely like a dream.
If the consciousness-mind is quiescent and there is not a single place where a thought moves, [then one is awakened].
This is called perfect awakening.
Question:
What is the measure of the manifestation of one's own mind?
Answer: One perceives that all phenomena exist;
yet they exist by virtue of their own non-existence.
One's own mind conceives of existence;
yet one sees that all phenomena are non-existent.
This non-existence is not itself non-existent.
One's own mind conceives of things as non-existent; even so it is with all phenomena—
they are all conceived as existent by one's own mind.
One's own mind conceives of them as non-existent;
furthermore, even if one commits all manner of sins,
one perceives oneself as the Dharma King.
One immediately attains liberation.
If one attains liberation through the practice of the physical body, one’s vital energy and strength will be robust.
One who perceives the Dharma through engagement maintains mindfulness at every stage;
one who understands through words [perceives it] through letters.
With weak physical strength,
one who acts in accordance with reality and the Dharma should deeply follow your various activities.
Leaping, bounding, tumbling, and falling—
all these neither go beyond the dharma-realm,
nor do they enter the dharma-realm.
If one enters the dharma-realm by means of the dharma-realm,
that person is a fool; whatever they perform will be in vain.
Ultimately, it does not depart from the mind of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-citta). Why is this?
Because the essence of the mind is the dharma-realm.
Question:
Worldly people engage in various studies;
why do they not attain the Way?
Answer: Because one perceives a self, one does not attain the Way.
"Self" refers to the ego.
The person of ultimate attainment encounters suffering without sorrow and meets joy without delight,
because they do not perceive a self.
The reason one does not perceive suffering or pleasure is that,
by having lost the sense of self,
one has attained the state of non-existence.
If even the self perishes,
what further thing could possibly not perish?
Question.
Since all phenomena are empty,
who is it that cultivates the path? Answer:
If there is someone,
who must cultivate the path?
If there is no one, [who must cultivate it]?
Then there would be no need to cultivate the Path.
Who is it that [cultivates]? It is "I" myself.
If there were no "I," [there would be no cultivation].
Upon encountering things, do not give rise to notions of right or wrong.
As for "right," it is simply that I myself consider it right,
while the thing itself is not right.
As for "not," it is that I myself am not;
yet things are not non-existent.
Thus, the mind is without mind.
This is what it means to penetrate the Buddha-way:
that things do not give rise to views is called penetrating the Way.
Encountering any object, one directly penetrates it to know its source;
such a person has opened the eye of wisdom.
The wise person follows things as they are and does not follow their own self.
Thus, there is neither grasping nor rejecting, neither opposition nor compliance.
When the ignorant act according to themselves and not according to things,

Among my ten great disciples, [he is the most grievous].
Ānanda was foremost in erudition,
yet he lacked true insight into the Buddha;
he merely pursued extensive learning.
Those of the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists all lack the recognition of the Buddha;
their cultivation and realization consist of calculating the numerical categories of consciousness, thereby falling into the realm of cause and effect.
This is the retribution for sentient beings;
they cannot escape birth and death and act in opposition to the Buddha’s intent.
This is precisely slandering the Buddha;
such sentient beings commit no transgression by being killed.
As the Sūtra says:
An icchantika does not give rise to faith;
therefore, there is no fault in killing them.
However, if they possess faith...
This person is one who occupies the rank of a Buddha.
If they have not yet seen their own nature,
they should not take it upon themselves to slander others as being good or virtuous.
To deceive oneself is of no benefit;
good and evil are clearly manifest,
and cause and effect are distinct.
Heaven and hell lie right before one's eyes;
yet the foolish do not believe.
Now they have fallen into the dark hells.
They neither perceive nor know this,
solely because their karma is heavy;
therefore, they do not believe.
For example, a person without eyes does not believe that there is light on the path;
even if one were to explain it to them, they would still not believe,
solely because they are blind.
By what means can one distinguish the sunlight?
So too it is with the foolish person;
they have now fallen among the various classes of animals.
Born into poverty and low station,
they seek life but cannot find it;
they seek death but cannot find it.
Although they undergo such suffering,
when questioned directly, they even say,
"I am happy now."
It is no different from heaven;
therefore, one knows that for all sentient beings,
their place of birth is a source of happiness.
They neither perceive nor know it;
such evil persons do so solely because their karmic obstructions are heavy.
The reason one is unable to give rise to faith is not due to external factors;
it is because one has not seen that one's own mind is the Buddha.
It does not consist in shaving off the hair and beard;
even those in white robes are Buddhas,
provided they have not failed to see their nature.
Shaving off the hair and beard is also [the practice of] non-Buddhists.
A question is asked:
"Laypeople have wives and children."
If lust is not eliminated,
by what means can one attain Buddhahood?
He replied:
It speaks only of seeing one's nature and does not mention lustful desire;
it is precisely because one has not seen one's nature that such desires arise.
Once one has attained the vision of one's true nature,
sexual desire is fundamentally empty;
it is quiescent and requires no deliberate severance.
Nor does one take delight in or become attached to them. Why?
Because their nature is fundamentally pure.
Although it dwells within the physical body of the five aggregates,
its nature is fundamentally pure and cannot be defiled.
The Dharma-body is fundamentally without sensation;
it has neither hunger nor thirst,
neither cold nor heat, and no illness.
Without cause, without craving,
without kin, and without suffering or pleasure.
There is no good or evil;
no long or short;
no strong or weak.
Originally, there is not a single thing that can be obtained.
It is solely because of the attachment to the existence of this physical body that there arise the manifestations of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, miasmic diseases, and so forth.
If one does not cling [to anything], then one may act as one pleases;
within the cycle of birth and death, one attains great mastery and transforms all phenomena.
He possesses the supernatural powers and mastery of the sages, being unimpeded and finding no place where he is not at ease.
Should there be any doubt in his mind, [he resolves it].
One will certainly fail to penetrate through all realms of experience;
even if one acts as if doing the best possible work,
one will not escape the cycle of birth and death.
If one realizes the nature [of reality], even a caṇḍāla can attain Buddhahood. Question:
Question: A candala performs the work of killing living beings;
how can such a person attain Buddhahood?
Answer: [As follows:]
It speaks only of seeing one's nature;
it does not speak of performing actions.
Even though the performance of actions may differ, [the nature remains the same].
All karma cannot constrain them;
from beginningless, vast kalpas past,
it has been solely because they have not seen their nature.
They fall into the hells.
Thus they create karma and cycle through birth and death;
yet from awakening, they attain their original nature.
One will ultimately not engage in [further] karma;
yet, if one does not realize the nature,
one cannot avoid retribution even by reciting the Buddha's name.
It is not that one intentionally kills living beings;
rather, if one sees their true nature, doubt is suddenly eliminated,
and even if one were to kill living beings, it could do nothing to them.
The twenty-seven patriarchs of India merely transmitted the mind-seal from one to another;
I have now come to this land.
It transmits only the One Mind;
it does not speak of precepts, giving,
diligence, or ascetic practices.
Even such practices as entering fire or water, climbing upon wheels of swords,
eating only once a day at dawn, observing the fast, and remaining seated without lying down—
all these are the conditioned dharmas of non-Buddhists.
If one realizes the nature of consciousness— the spirit and awareness that functions through giving and movement—
that is the mind of all Buddhas;
from the Buddhas of the past to those of the future, they speak only of transmitting this mind.
There is no other dharma apart from this.
If one recognizes this dharma,
even an ordinary person who does not recognize a single character is a Buddha.
If one does not recognize the nature of one's own numinous awareness,
even if one were to break one's body into particles as fine as motes of dust in search of the Buddha,
one would ultimately find nothing.
The Buddha is also called the Dharma-body,
and is also called the original mind.
This mind has no form or characteristics.
It is without cause or effect;
it is without sinews or bones;
it is like empty space.
It cannot be grasped;
it is not of the nature of material obstruction,
nor is it like that of the non-Buddhists.
This mind can be fully realized only by the Tathāgata alone;
all other sentient beings, being deluded, do not clearly understand it.
This mind is never separate from the physical body composed of the four great elements.
If one is separated from this mind,
there is no capacity for movement;
this body is devoid of cognition.
Like grass, trees, tiles, or rubble,
the body is insentient;
by what cause does it move?
If one's own mind moves,
even down to speech, purposeful activity, motion, seeing,
hearing, sensing, and knowing.
All are movements of the mind;
the movement of the mind functions through movement,
and movement is its very function.
Movement is not external to the mind;
the mind is not external to movement.
Movement is not the mind.
The mind does not move;
movement is fundamentally without mind,
and the mind is fundamentally without movement.
Movement does not depart from the mind;
the mind does not depart from movement.
Movement is never separate from the mind.
The mind is devoid of movement and departure;
movement is the function of the mind,
and function is the movement of the mind.
It moves and it functions;
it does not move and it does not function.
The essence of its functioning is fundamentally empty.
Space is fundamentally without movement;
movement and function share the same essence as the mind.
The mind is fundamentally without movement.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Though moving, there is no movement;
thus, though seeing all day long, one has never seen."
All day long one hears, yet has never heard;
all day long one perceives, yet has never perceived;
all day long one knows, yet has never known.
Throughout the day one walks and sits, yet has never walked or sat;
throughout the day one is angry and joyful, yet has never been angry or joyful.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
The path of language is cut off;
the sphere of mental activity ceases;
seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing [are extinguished].
It is fundamentally and originally in a state of perfect stillness.
Even as for anger, joy, pain, and itching—how are they different from a wooden man?
It is simply because, when one investigates them, pain and itching cannot be found.
The Sūtra says:
"Evil karma immediately results in bitter retribution;
virtuous karma immediately results in wholesome retribution."
Not only does anger lead to falling into hell,
but joy leads to rebirth in heaven;
yet if one knows that the nature of both anger and joy is empty, [one is liberated].
However, non-attachment does not mean that one is liberated from all karma;
if one recites the sutras without seeing their true nature,
there is absolutely no basis for it.
The exposition is likewise inexhaustible;
this brief indication of the false and the correct is but a fraction of it,
not even one or two parts.
A verse was spoken:
"I have come to this land To transmit the Dharma and save deluded minds.
When the flower blooms in five petals, The fruit will naturally be formed."
The river raft parts the jade waves; the torches open the golden locks.
Five mouths travel together; for ninety years there has been no "self" or "other. The discourse on the life-force (blood-veins) is now concluded.
